title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
gist: Amazon researchers present HOPE, a second-order method that prunes Mixture-of-Experts models by accounting for pairwise expert co-activation instead of scoring experts independently. At 50% pruning it matched the unpruned Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on SWE-Bench Pro (42.3 vs 41.8) while the REAP baseline fell to 36.2.

insights.claim: In MoE LLMs every expert MLP must sit in memory at inference even though most are idle per token; Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of 48 MoE layers, uses only 8 per token, and expert MLPs take about 95% of its ~250 GB parameter footprint.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Expert memory, not compute, is the serving cost driver for large MoEs, so compression directly lowers hardware needs.

insights.claim: Expert pruning is favored over dynamic expert loading/off-loading because it avoids latency issues, needs no training and composes with quantization.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Pruning plus quantization is a stackable route to cheaper inference of large MoE models.
insights.locator: Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes

insights.claim: At 50% pruning, memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning and more tool calls, making it the most deployment-relevant setting.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Freed memory can be reallocated to agentic workloads, improving serving economics.
insights.locator: At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves

insights.claim: Existing expert-pruning methods are first-order: they assign each expert an independent scalar importance from calibration data and cut the lowest per layer, ignoring that experts form stable cooperative groups that are co-activated together.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Core critique of the incumbent approach, suggesting gaps in current compression tooling.
insights.locator: Existing pruning methods score each expert independently

insights.claim: Removing an expert that looks unimportant alone can dismantle a cooperative group if a partner that relies on it is highly important, and this effect compounds at high pruning rates where many cooperative links break.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Explains why naive pruning degrades sharply at aggressive rates.

insights.claim: HOPE minimizes a tractable surrogate that upper-bounds the dominant pruning error, whose squared-sum form yields pairwise cross-terms; the prune-set is found by a quadratic program over an expert-by-expert interaction matrix F solved via continuous relaxation.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Pairwise interaction modeling is tractable at small cost, so it is practical to adopt.

insights.claim: HOPE needs the same single calibration forward pass as other methods; the extra QP solve takes 1-2 seconds per layer, making overhead negligible.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Better pruning quality at essentially no added compute cost.

insights.claim: The diagonal of HOPE's F-matrix recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman 0.988), so HOPE's gains over REAP are attributable to the off-diagonal interaction terms.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Cleanly isolates the value of second-order information.

insights.claim: Across 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, GLM-4.5-Air), 2 calibration sets and 4 first-order baselines, HOPE had the best average rank (2.07 of 5), with top-1 in 39% of conditions and top-2 in 67%.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Gains are consistent but modest overall, so the case rests on aggressive-pruning regimes.

insights.claim: At 50% pruning HOPE's average rank is 1.58 versus 2.42 for the next-best method REAP, and its advantage grows as pruning rate rises.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Largest edge is where memory savings matter most.

insights.claim: On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE scored 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned 41.8, while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Half the experts removed with no agentic-coding loss would materially cut serving cost.

insights.claim: HOPE's advantage is largest on agentic coding because such multi-turn tasks combining coding, tool calls and reasoning likely exercise diverse expert combinations where preserving cooperative structure matters most.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads are more sensitive to pruning choices than simple benchmarks.
insights.locator: HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro

insights.claim: Pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because removing low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks, an effect seen across pruning methods.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Suggests MoE models carry redundancy that can be exploited, though the explanation is speculative.
insights.quote: likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks
insights.locator: Notably, pruned models can occasionally match

insights.claim: Code-focused calibration with any pruning method, including HOPE, did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well on the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Domain-specific pruning for coding agents looks low-risk for general capability.

insights.claim: Experts retained only by HOPE have higher cooperative scores than those retained only by REAP, meaning HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts to preserve cooperative clusters, and benchmark gains validate the trade-off.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Individual importance is a misleading pruning criterion; group structure matters.

insights.claim: The pruned output is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint, smaller on disk and in memory, needing no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions; the package is tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5 and GLM-4.5.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Drop-in compatibility with common serving stacks lowers adoption friction.

insights.claim: HOPE's advantage shrinks at low pruning rates (10-20%) where first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive; it also prunes layers independently, with cross-layer HOPE preliminary, and does not capture triplet or higher interactions, which are combinatorially hard to estimate.
insights.speaker: Alex M Tseng
insights.so_what: Benefit is regime-specific; further gains from cross-layer and higher-order modeling remain unproven.
